en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 72.
The Training Rule on Remorse.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was speaking to the bhikkhus on many occasions about the discipline (vinaya),
praising the discipline, praising the mastery of the discipline, and repeatedly praising the Venerable Upāli.
The bhikkhus thought:
“The Blessed One has indeed spoken on the discourse of the Vinaya in many ways; he has praised the Vinaya and praised the mastery of the Vinaya, repeatedly extolling the venerable Upāli.

Come now, friends, let us master the Vinaya in the presence of the venerable Upāli. And so, many bhikkhus—seniors, juniors, and those of middle standing—mastered the Vinaya in the presence of the venerable Upāli.
Then it occurred to the group-of-six bhikkhus:
“Friends, at present many bhikkhus—seniors, juniors, and those of middle standing—are mastering the Vinaya in the presence of the Venerable Upāli.
If they become experts in the Vinaya, they will drag us about and harass us as they please, as they wish, and for as long as they like.
Come, friends, let us disparage the Vinaya.”
Then the group-of-six monks approached other monks and said this:
"What is the use of reciting these minor and lesser training rules, which lead only to remorse, vexation, and anxiety?
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How can the group of six monks disparage the Vinaya? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you disparage the Vinaya?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, disparage the Vinaya?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“If any monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should speak thus:

‘What is the use of reciting these minor and lesser training rules, which lead only to remorse, vexation, and irritation?’—for one who disparages the training rules, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).”
"But whoever" means whoever such [a person]...
"monks" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
"While the Pātimokkha is being recited" means while it is being recited, or caused to be recited, or while it is being rehearsed.
"He would speak thus":
"But what is the use of these minor and lesser training rules being recited, since they lead only to remorse, vexation, and distress?
"Those who master this have remorse; they have vexation; they have distress; those who do not..."
For those who master it, there is no remorse, no vexation, and no distress. "It would be better if this were not recited;
it would be better if this were not upheld; it would be better if this were not mastered; it would be better if this were not borne in mind.
Either the Vinaya should disappear, or these monks should remain ungrateful"—thus [he speaks] regarding the Vinaya for one who is fully ordained.

If one disparages the Vinaya regarding one who is fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If one disparages the Vinaya regarding one who is fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If one disparages the Vinaya regarding one who is fully ordained, being uncertain of their status, there is an offense of expiation.
If one disparages the Vinaya while perceiving a person who is fully ordained as not being fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one disparages another teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one disparages either the Vinaya or another teaching to a person who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, but one perceives them as ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] is not ordained, but one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, and one perceives them as not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

There is no offense if he does not wish to disparage [the Vinaya], but says, "Come now, you should master the Suttantas, the Gāthās, or the Abhidhamma; afterwards you will master the Vinaya," or if he is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The second training rule on disparaging is finished.
